items.question: Where and as what should the goddess be visualized at the outset of this practice?
premises: The visualization occurs in the mūlādhāra.
The locus is a four-petaled lotus.
The form is likened to a child's two breasts.
items.inference: The practitioner should remember the goddess in the four-petaled lotus of the mūlādhāra as like a child's breasts.
items.plain_english: One should remember her in the four-petaled lotus of the mūlādhāra, like the two breasts of a child.

items.question: What luminous and dynamic form does the goddess assume in this visualization?
premises: The goddess is composed of three whirls.
Her essential form is a mass of lightning.
items.inference: The goddess is to be contemplated as three-whirled and radiant like a cluster of lightning.
items.plain_english: One should remember the goddess as made of three whirls and having the form of a mass of lightning.

items.question: How is the goddess characterized in subtlety and power over the six wheels?
premises: The goddess is subtler than the subtle.
She pierces the six wheels.
items.inference: The goddess is both supremely subtle and capable of penetrating all six cakras.
items.plain_english: One should remember the goddess as subtler than the subtle and as the piercer of the six wheels.

items.question: Which petal letters must be gathered into the lotus womb during this stage?
premises: The letters range from va to sa.
These letters are situated on the petals.
They are to be gathered in the lotus womb.
items.inference: The practitioner should gather the petal letters from va to sa into the lotus womb.
items.plain_english: One should gather the letters situated on the petals, from va to sa, into the womb of the lotus.

items.question: What action must the teacher perform in the svādhiṣṭhāna after proper joining?
premises: The locus is the svādhiṣṭhāna.
The teacher first joins properly.
After joining, piercing is performed.
items.inference: Having properly joined in the svādhiṣṭhāna, the teacher should pierce it.
items.plain_english: In the svādhiṣṭhāna, the teacher, having properly joined, should then pierce.

items.question: Which petaled center joined with specific letters must be pierced by oneself?
premises: The center is ten-petaled.
It is joined with letters from ḍa to pha.
The piercing is done by oneself.
items.inference: One should pierce the ten-petaled center joined with the letters from ḍa to pha.
items.plain_english: One should oneself pierce the ten-petaled center joined with the letters from ḍa to pha.

items.question: What lotus associated with letters from ka to ṭha must be pierced in the īśvara center?
premises: The lotus has petals with letters from ka to ṭha.
The action occurs in the īśvara center.
The piercing is done by oneself.
items.inference: One should pierce the lotus bearing letters from ka to ṭha in the īśvara center.
uncertainties: īśvare may name a center or a deity-locus; taken as locus here
items.plain_english: One should oneself pierce, in the īśvara center, the lotus whose petals bear the letters from ka to ṭha.

items.question: What elements must be carefully joined in the lotus whose petals consist of kalās?
premises: The lotus has petals made of kalās.
The vowels are to be joined there.
The joining must be done carefully.
items.inference: One should carefully join the vowels in the lotus whose petals are made of kalās.
items.plain_english: Having carefully joined the vowels in the lotus whose petals are made of kalās.

items.question: Which two-petaled center must the teacher pierce after joining ha and kṣa?
premises: The center is two-petaled.
It is joined with ha and kṣa.
The teacher performs the piercing.
items.inference: The teacher, having pierced the two-petaled center joined with ha and kṣa, proceeds further.
items.plain_english: Then the teacher, having pierced the two-petaled center joined with ha and kṣa.

items.question: Into which successive subtle stages must kalā and nāda be merged in sequence?
premises: Kalā is joined into nāda.
Nāda is joined into nādānta.
The process proceeds sequentially.
items.inference: The practitioner merges kalā into nāda and then nāda into nādānta.
items.plain_english: Having joined kalā into nāda, and again joined nāda into nādānta.

items.question: What must the teacher withdraw into his own mouth at this culminating stage?
premises: The object is the viṣuvaktra.
The locus is the teacher's own mouth.
The teacher performs the withdrawal himself.
items.inference: The teacher should withdraw the viṣuvaktra into his own mouth.
uncertainties: viṣuvaktraṃ is a technical term; rendered literally as equinoctial-opening
items.plain_english: The teacher himself should withdraw the viṣuvaktra into his own mouth.

items.question: What transformation occurs in the disciple on earth through the teacher's command?
premises: The disciple acts under the teacher's command.
At that time the disciple's ignorance is burnt.
This occurs on earth.
items.inference: By the power of the teacher's command, the disciple's ignorance is burnt while still on earth.
items.plain_english: Then, by the power of the teacher's command, the disciple on earth has his ignorance burnt away.

items.question: What identity does the disciple attain as a result of this initiation process?
premises: The disciple may become Sadāśiva himself.
This is asserted as true.
There is no doubt about it.
items.inference: The disciple truly becomes Sadāśiva himself, without doubt.
items.plain_english: He himself becomes Sadāśiva; this is truly so, without doubt.

items.question: How many initiations have been declared and what is their proper effect?
premises: Four initiations are thus declared.
They are properly auspicious-bringing.
items.inference: Four initiations have been declared, and they properly bring auspiciousness.
items.plain_english: Thus four initiations have been declared, which properly bring auspiciousness.

items.question: What form of initiation is constituted when the teacher touches the disciple's body?
premises: The teacher touches the disciple's body.
This act defines a specific initiation.
items.inference: When the teacher touches the disciple's body, it is called sparśadīkṣā.
items.plain_english: If the teacher touches the disciple's body, this is touch-initiation.

items.question: What form of initiation is defined by the utterance of joined mantras?
premises: Joined mantras are uttered.
This act is given a specific name.
items.inference: The utterance of joined mantras is called vāgdīkṣā.
items.plain_english: If he utters joined mantras, it is called speech-initiation.

items.question: What initiation arises when the teacher properly looks upon the disciple?
premises: The teacher properly sees the disciple.
This act constitutes a named initiation.
The address is to the beloved.
items.inference: When the teacher properly looks at the disciple, that is dṛgdīkṣā.
items.plain_english: If the teacher properly looks upon the disciple, that would be sight-initiation, O beloved.

items.question: Which initiation is recognized when knowledge arises immediately in the disciple?
premises: Knowledge arises immediately.
That arising is identified as an initiation.
It is considered śāmbhavī.
items.inference: The initiation in which knowledge arises immediately is considered śāmbhavī.
items.plain_english: When knowledge arises immediately, that initiation is considered śāmbhavī.

items.question: Why do mantras taught without proper transmission become fruitless?
premises: Some mantras may be taught without the required mediation.
Such mantras become fruitless.
A reason is being given.
items.inference: Mantras taught without proper transmission are fruitless for that reason.
uncertainties: antareṇa implies absence of proper instruction/transmission context
items.plain_english: Because mantras that are taught without proper transmission would be fruitless.

items.question: What qualifications must the recipient possess before receiving the transmitted teaching?
premises: The recipient must know teacher, mantra, and tradition.
The recipient must protect vow-conduct.
items.inference: The teaching is to be given to one who knows the guru, mantra, and āgama and who upholds the observances.
items.plain_english: To one who knows the teacher, mantra, and tradition, and who guards the observance of the vows.

items.question: After what period of preparation should the teaching be entrusted to a worthy disciple?
premises: This is done for some time.
After doing this, transmission occurs.
The recipient is a good disciple.
items.inference: After maintaining this for some time, one should entrust it to a worthy disciple.
uncertainties: aitat refers back to prior preparation/training
items.plain_english: Having done this for some time, one should entrust it to a good disciple.

items.question: What ultimate result follows proper transmission according to Śaṅkara's statement?
premises: The sequence leads to a result.
The result is eternal liberation.
This is spoken by Śaṅkara.
items.inference: Proper transmission leads to eternal liberation, as stated by Śaṅkara.
items.plain_english: Then there is eternal liberation — thus it was spoken by Śaṅkara.

items.question: What responsibility does the teacher bear toward the lineage of transmission?
premises: The tradition must remain unbroken.
The teacher is the agent responsible.
This must be done always.
items.inference: The teacher should always keep the tradition unbroken.
items.plain_english: The teacher should always keep the tradition unbroken, O beloved.

items.question: What consequence follows if the mantra is taught without observing the proper sequence?
premises: The mantra should be taught afterwards.
An alternative condition is considered.
Otherwise it becomes fruitless.
items.inference: If the mantra is not taught in the proper sequence, it becomes fruitless.
items.plain_english: Afterwards one should teach the mantra; otherwise it would be fruitless.
